title: Data Management

toc.title: DATA MANAGEMENT CHALLENGES (13 Challenges — Know the Key Ones)

html:
CDMP Fundamentals Exam Study Summary

1CORE DEFINITIONS (High Exam Priority)

Term Definition
Data Management The development, execution, and supervision of plans, policies, programs, and practices that deliver, control, protect, and enhance the value of data and information assets throughout their lifecycles.
Data Management Professional Any person who works in any facet of data management — from highly technical (DBA, programmer) to strategic business roles (Data Steward, CDO, Data Strategist).
Asset An economic resource that can be owned or controlled and that holds or produces value. Assets can be converted to money.
Data Lifecycle Based on the product lifecycle (NOT the systems development lifecycle). Includes: Plan → Design & Enable → Create/Obtain → Store/Maintain → Enhance → Use → Dispose of.
Data Strategy A set of choices and decisions that chart a high-level course of action to achieve high-level goals. Must come from understanding the data needs inherent in business strategy.
Data ROT Data that is Redundant, Obsolete, Trivial — organizations should minimize ROT as part of lifecycle management.
Information Gaps The difference between what we know and what we need to know to make an effective decision. Represent enterprise liabilities.
Exam tip

The definition of Data Management is frequently tested. Know every word — especially "throughout their lifecycles."

2DATA MANAGEMENT GOALS (Know All 6)

Within an organization, data management goals include:

  1. Understanding and supporting the information needs of the enterprise and its stakeholders
  2. Capturing, storing, protecting, and ensuring the integrity of data assets
  3. Ensuring the quality of data and information
  4. Ensuring privacy and confidentiality of stakeholder data
  5. Preventing unauthorized or inappropriate access, manipulation, or use of data
  6. Ensuring data can be used effectively to add value to the enterprise

3DATA — ESSENTIAL CONCEPTS

3.1 What is Data?

  • Data represents facts about the world stored in digital (or paper) form
  • Data is both:
    • An interpretation of the objects it represents
    • An object that must be interpreted (requires context to be meaningful)
  • Context = data's representational system (common vocabulary + relationships)
  • Conventions of the representational system are documented as Metadata

3.2 Data vs. Information

  • Data = "raw material of information"; Information = "data in context"
  • The DIKW pyramid (Data → Information → Knowledge → Wisdom) has 3 limitations:
    1. Assumes data simply exists — but data must be created
    2. Fails to recognize that knowledge is needed to create data in the first place
    3. Implies data and information are separate, when in reality they are intertwined
  • Throughout DMBOK, "data" and "information" are used interchangeably

3.3 Data as an Organizational Asset

  • Data is widely recognized as an enterprise asset
  • Being data-driven means: using event triggers and analytics for actionable insight instead of gut feelings
  • Businesses must co-create information solutions with technical data professionals and line-of-business counterparts
  • Data monetization is becoming increasingly common (may appear on P&L statements)
Exam tip

Data is NOT consumed when it is used — this is the key differentiator from physical/financial assets.

4DATA MANAGEMENT PRINCIPLES (Know All 11)

Exam tip

These are frequently tested — memorize the groupings shown in Figure 1.

Group 1: Data is Valuable

  1. Data is an asset with unique properties — not tangible, not consumed when used, durable, easy to copy/transport, can be used by multiple people simultaneously
  2. The value of data can and should be expressed in economic terms — organizations should develop consistent ways to quantify value; measure costs of low quality AND benefits of high quality

Group 2: Data Management Requirements are Business Requirements

  1. Managing data means managing the quality of data — ensuring data is fit for purpose is a primary goal
  2. It takes Metadata to manage data — Metadata is the data used to manage and use data; originates from architecture, modeling, stewardship, governance, DQ management, systems development, IT/business operations, and analytics
  3. It takes planning to manage data — requires architectural and process planning
  4. Data management requirements must drive IT decisions — technology should serve, not drive, data needs

Group 3: Data Management Depends on Diverse Skills

  1. Data management is cross-functional — requires both technical and non-technical skills and collaboration
  2. Data management requires an enterprise perspective — must be applied across the enterprise; this is why data management and data governance are intertwined
  3. Data management must account for a range of perspectives — data is fluid; must evolve with how data is created and used

Group 4: Data Management is Lifecycle Management

  1. Different types of data have different lifecycle characteristics — and therefore different management requirements
  2. Managing data includes managing the risks associated with data — data can be lost, stolen, or misused; ethical implications must be considered

Group 5: Effective Data Management Requires Leadership Commitment

  • Effective data management requires leadership commitment — requires coordination, collaboration, commitment, vision, and purpose

5DATA MANAGEMENT CHALLENGES (13 Challenges — Know the Key Ones)

5.1 Data Differs from Other Assets

  • Data is not tangible, yet durable (doesn't wear out)
  • Easy to copy and transport, but not easy to reproduce if lost/destroyed
  • Not consumed when used — can be stolen without being gone
  • Can be used by multiple people simultaneously — impossible with physical/financial assets
  • Most uses of data beget more data — volumes keep increasing

5.2 Data Valuation

  • Value = difference between cost and benefit
  • Data valuation is complicated because neither costs nor benefits are standardized
  • Data value is contextual (varies by organization) and often temporal (changes over time)
  • Sample cost/benefit categories:
    • Cost of obtaining and storing data
    • Cost of replacing data if lost
    • Impact if data were missing
    • Cost of risk mitigation
    • Cost of improving data
    • Benefits of higher quality data
    • What competitors would pay for data
    • What data could be sold for
    • Expected revenue from innovative uses

5.3 Data Quality

  • Poor quality data costs organizations 10–30% of revenue to handle
  • IBM estimated cost of poor quality data in US (2016): $3.1 Trillion
  • Costs of poor quality data:
    • Scrap and rework
    • Work-arounds and hidden correction processes
    • Organizational inefficiencies / low productivity
    • Organizational conflict
    • Low job satisfaction
    • Customer dissatisfaction
    • Opportunity costs / inability to innovate
    • Compliance costs or fines
    • Reputational costs
  • Benefits of high quality data:
    • Improved customer experience, higher productivity, reduced risk
    • Ability to act on opportunities, increased revenue, competitive advantage

5.4 Planning for Better Data

  • Deriving value from data does not happen by accident — requires planning
  • Organizations should view data as a product they create
  • Requires systems thinking around: how data connects processes, relationship between processes and technology, design and architecture, strategic use of data

5.5 Metadata and Data Management

  • Metadata describes what data an org has, what it represents, classification, origin, movement, evolution, access rights, and quality
  • Metadata is a form of data and must be managed as such
  • Metadata management often provides a starting point for improvements in data management overall

5.6 Data Management is Cross-functional

  • Requires: design skills, technical skills, data analysis skills, analytic skills, language skills (consensus on definitions), strategic thinking

5.7 Establishing an Enterprise Perspective

  • Data is one of the 'horizontals' of an organization — moves across verticals
  • Data is often viewed as a by-product of operational processes — not planned beyond immediate need
  • One reason data governance is important — helps organizations make decisions about data across verticals

5.8 Accounting for Other Perspectives

  • Organizations use internal AND externally acquired data
  • Must account for legal and compliance requirements across national and industry lines
  • People who create data often forget someone else will use it later

5.9 The Data Lifecycle

  • Data lifecycle is based on the product lifecycle (not SDLC)
  • Data has lineage — a pathway from point of origin to point of usage (also called the data chain)
  • Key implications:
    • Creation and usage are the most critical points in the lifecycle
    • Data Quality must be managed throughout the lifecycle
    • Metadata Quality must be managed throughout the lifecycle
    • Data Security must be managed throughout the lifecycle — from creation to disposal
    • Focus on most critical data — minimize ROT (Redundant, Obsolete, Trivial)

5.10 Different Types of Data

  • Data classified by: type (transactional, Reference, Master, Metadata), content (domains, subject areas), format, protection level, storage/access method
  • Master Data has different uses and management requirements than transactional data

5.11 Data and Risk

  • Organizations get most value from data that is: available, relevant, complete, accurate, consistent, timely, usable, meaningful, and understood
  • Key regulations mentioned: Sarbanes-Oxley, Solvency II, data privacy regulations

5.12 Data Management and Technology

  • Managing technology is NOT the same as managing data
  • Data requirements aligned with business strategy should drive technology decisions — not the reverse

5.13 Effective Data Management Requires Leadership and Commitment

  • Leader's Data Manifesto (2017): "An organization's best opportunities for organic growth lie in data"
  • Chief Data Officer (CDO) role stems from recognition that data management must be business-driven, not IT-driven
  • CDO leads: data management initiatives AND cultural change

6DATA MANAGEMENT STRATEGY

Components of a Data Management Strategy (Know These)

  1. A compelling vision for data management
  2. A summary business case with examples
  3. Guiding principles, values, and management perspectives
  4. The mission and long-term directional goals
  5. Proposed measures of success
  6. Short-term (12–24 months) SMART objectives (Specific, Measurable, Actionable, Realistic, Time-bound)
  7. Descriptions of roles and organizations with responsibilities and decision rights
  8. Descriptions of program components and initiatives
  9. A prioritized program of work with scope boundaries
  10. A draft implementation roadmap

Key Deliverables from Strategic Planning

Deliverable Description
Data Management Charter Overall vision, business case, goals, guiding principles, measures of success, risks, operating model
Data Management Scope Statement Goals and objectives for a planning horizon (usually 3 years), roles and accountable leaders
Data Management Implementation Roadmap Specific programs, projects, task assignments, delivery milestones
Exam tip

Strategy is often owned by the CDO and enacted through a data governance team, supported by a Data Governance Council.

7DATA MANAGEMENT FRAMEWORKS

7.1 Strategic Alignment Model (Henderson & Venkatraman, 1999)

  • Abstracts the fundamental drivers for any approach to data management
  • Center: relationship between data (associated with IT and physical systems) and information (associated with business strategy and operational use)
  • Four fundamental domains: Business Strategy, IT Strategy, Organizational Infrastructure & Processes, IT Infrastructure & Processes

7.2 Amsterdam Information Model (AIM) — "The 9-Cell"

  • (Abcouwer, Maes, Truijens, 1997)
  • Recognizes a middle layer focusing on structure and tactics (planning and architecture)
  • Recognizes the necessity of information communication (information governance and data quality pillar)
  • Three levels: Strategy, Tactics, Operations
  • Three columns: Business, Information, IT

7.3 The DAMA-DMBOK Framework

Three visual components:

Visual Purpose
DAMA Wheel (Figure 5) Defines the 11 Knowledge Areas; Data Governance at the center
Environmental Factors Hexagon (Figure 6) Shows relationship between people, process, technology; Goals & Principles at the center
Knowledge Area Context Diagram (Figure 7) SIPOC-based; details each KA — definition, goals, activities, inputs, deliverables, roles, suppliers, consumers, participants, tools, techniques, metrics

Context Diagram — 4 Activity Categories

Code Category Description
(P) Planning Set strategic/tactical course; occur on a recurring basis
(D) Development Organized around SDLC (analysis, design, build, test, preparation, deployment)
(C) Control Ensure ongoing quality, integrity, reliability, and security
(O) Operational Support use, maintenance, and enhancement of systems and processes

Context Diagram — 12 Components

  1. Definition, 2. Goals, 3. Activities, 4. Inputs, 5. Deliverables, 6. Roles & Responsibilities, 7. Suppliers, 8. Consumers, 9. Participants, 10. Tools, 11. Techniques, 12. Metrics
Exam tip

Know the difference: Suppliers provide/enable access to inputs. Consumers benefit from deliverables. Participants perform, manage, or approve activities.

7.4 DMBOK Pyramid (Aiken)

Four phases an organization goes through:

  • Phase 1: Purchase application → Data Modeling, Storage, Security, Integration/Interoperability
  • Phase 2: Address Data Quality challenges → Need reliable Metadata and consistent Data Architecture
  • Phase 3: Data Governance provides structural support → enables MDM, DW/BI, Reference Data, Document & Content
  • Phase 4: Leverage well-managed data → advance analytic capabilities (the "golden pyramid")

7.5 DAMA Data Management Framework Evolved (Geuens)

  • BI/Analytics depends on all other functions
  • Depends on Master Data and Data Warehouse solutions
  • Those depend on feeding systems and applications
  • Foundation: Data Quality, Data Design, Data Interoperability
  • Data Governance (including Metadata, Security, Architecture, Reference Data) provides foundation for ALL other functions

8THE 11 KNOWLEDGE AREAS (DAMA Wheel)

Exam tip

Know the chapter number, definition, and which chapters cover which topics.

# Knowledge Area Chapter Key Definition
1 Data Governance 3 Direction and oversight for data management; establishes a system of decision rights
2 Data Architecture 4 Blueprint for managing data assets by aligning with organizational strategy
3 Data Modeling & Design 5 Discovering, analyzing, representing, and communicating data requirements in a data model
4 Data Storage & Operations 6 Design, implementation, and support of stored data to maximize its value; supports the full lifecycle
5 Data Security 7 Ensures privacy and confidentiality; prevents breaches; ensures appropriate access
6 Data Integration & Interoperability 8 Movement and consolidation of data within and between data stores, applications, and organizations
7 Document & Content Management 9 Manages unstructured media lifecycle; especially for legal and regulatory compliance
8 Reference & Master Data 10 Ongoing reconciliation of core critical shared data; ensures most accurate, timely, relevant version of truth
9 Data Warehousing & Business Intelligence 11 Manages decision support data; enables knowledge workers to get value via analysis and reporting
10 Metadata 12 Access to high quality, integrated Metadata; definitions, models, data flows
11 Data Quality 13 Planning and implementation of quality management techniques to measure, assess, and improve fitness of data

Additional DMBOK Chapters (Non-KA)

Chapter Topic
2 Data Handling Ethics
14 Big Data and Data Science
15 Data Management Maturity Assessment
16 Data Management Organization and Role Expectations
17 Data Management and Organizational Change Management

9DAMA INTERNATIONAL & DMBOK PURPOSE

The DMBOK supports DAMA's mission by:

  1. Providing a functional framework for enterprise data management practices (guiding principles, methods, roles, deliverables, metrics)
  2. Establishing a common vocabulary for data management concepts and serving as basis for best practices
  3. Serving as the fundamental reference guide for the CDMP and other certification exams
Exam tip

Data Governance is at the center of the DAMA Wheel — it provides consistency within and balance between all other Knowledge Areas.

10HIGH-PROBABILITY EXAM QUESTIONS

Q1. What is the formal DAMA definition of Data Management?

Development, execution, and supervision of plans, policies, programs, and practices that deliver, control, protect, and enhance the value of data and information assets throughout their lifecycles.

Q2. What is a key property that makes data different from physical and financial assets?

Data is not consumed when it is used. It can also be used by multiple people simultaneously.

Q3. The data lifecycle is based on which lifecycle?

The product lifecycle — NOT the systems development lifecycle (SDLC).

Q4. What does SMART stand for in the context of data management objectives?

Specific, Measurable, Actionable, Realistic, Time-bound

Q5. Which Knowledge Area is at the center of the DAMA Wheel and why?

Data Governance — because governance is required for consistency within and balance between all other functions.

Q6. What are the three deliverables from strategic planning for data management?

Data Management Charter, Data Management Scope Statement, Data Management Implementation Roadmap

Q7. IBM estimated the cost of poor quality data in the US in 2016 was how much?

$3.1 Trillion

Q8. What does Data ROT stand for?

Data that is Redundant, Obsolete, Trivial

Q9. What is at the center of the Environmental Factors Hexagon?

Goals and Principles

Q10. What are the four activity categories in a Knowledge Area Context Diagram?

Plan (P), Develop (D), Operate (O), Control (C)

Q11. The Amsterdam Information Model is also known as what?

The 9-cell model. Developed by Abcouwer, Maes, and Truijens (1997).

Q12. Who typically owns the data management strategy?

The Chief Data Officer (CDO), enacted through a data governance team supported by a Data Governance Council.

Q13. What are the three visual components of the DAMA-DMBOK Framework?

The DAMA Wheel, the Environmental Factors Hexagon, and the Knowledge Area Context Diagram

Q14. In the Context Diagram, what is the difference between Suppliers, Consumers, and Participants?

Suppliers provide or enable access to inputs. Consumers directly benefit from deliverables. Participants perform, manage performance of, or approve activities.

Q15. What is the planning horizon typically used in a Data Management Scope Statement?

3 years

Q16. What is the primary driver for data management according to DMBOK2?

To enable organizations to get value from their data assets, just as effective management of financial and physical assets enables organizations to get value from those assets.

Q17. According to the Leader's Data Manifesto (2017), where does an organization's best opportunity for organic growth lie?

In data.

Q18. Why was the CDO role created?

Stemmed from recognition that managing data presents unique challenges and that successful data management must be business-driven, not IT-driven. The CDO leads both data management initiatives AND cultural change.

Q19. What does the DIKW pyramid stand for and what are its three limitations per DMBOK?

Data, Information, Knowledge, Wisdom. Limitations: (1) assumes data simply exists — but it must be created; (2) fails to recognize knowledge is needed to create data; (3) implies data and information are separate when they are intertwined.

Q20. What are the two key regulations mentioned in DMBOK Chapter 1 related to data risk?

Sarbanes-Oxley (accuracy/validity of financial transaction data) and Solvency II (data lineage and quality underpinning risk models in insurance).
